title: Chain rule
applies: The outer and inner functions are differentiable at the relevant inputs.
steps: Identify the outer and inner functions.
Differentiate the outer function while leaving the inner expression in place.
Multiply by the derivative of the inner function.
pitfalls: A power rule on a composite still needs the inner derivative.
checks: At a point where the inner derivative is zero and the outer derivative is finite, the composite derivative should be zero.

title: Implicit differentiation
aliases: dy dx on an implicit curve
tangent slope without solving for y
pattern: F_x + F_y y′ = 0, so y′ = −F_x/F_y when F_y ≠ 0.
applies: F is continuously differentiable near the point, F=0 there, and F_y ≠ 0 for a locally differentiable y(x).
steps: Treat y as a function of x.
Differentiate the entire equation using product and chain rules.
Collect the y′ terms and solve before substituting the point.
pitfalls: Differentiate xy as y+xy′.
A zero coefficient of y′ requires separate tangent analysis.
checks: Verify the point satisfies the original equation.

title: L’Hôpital’s rule
pattern: For a qualifying 0/0 or ∞/∞ form, replace f/g by f′/g′ inside the limit.
applies: The functions are differentiable on a punctured one-sided interval, g′ is nonzero there, and the derivative quotient has a limit or diverges to signed infinity.
steps: Confirm the indeterminate form.
Differentiate numerator and denominator separately.
Recheck the form before another application. For a two-sided limit, check both sides.
pitfalls: The rule uses separate derivatives. A quotient-rule derivative answers a different question.
Products and differences need a valid quotient rewrite first.
checks: Check domain restrictions and any cancellation used in the derivative quotient.

title: Absolute extrema on a closed interval
pattern: For continuous f on [a,b], compare f at the endpoints and at all interior critical points.
applies: The function is continuous on the entire closed, bounded interval.
steps: Find interior points where f′ is zero or undefined.
Evaluate f at those points and both endpoints.
Compare values and list every point attaining either extreme.
pitfalls: An interior critical point need not be an extremum.
Endpoint values can tie interior values.
checks: Keep the location and the function value distinct.

example.problem: Find the absolute extrema of x³−3x²+1 on [−1,3].
example.answer: Minimum −3 at x=−1 and x=2. Maximum 1 at x=0 and x=3.

title: Integration by substitution
pattern: If u=g(x), then ∫ f(g(x))g′(x) dx = ∫ f(u) du.
applies: The integrand can be rewritten in one new variable and the functions satisfy the substitution rule on the interval.
steps: Choose an inner expression u and calculate du.
Rewrite all factors and change the bounds for a definite integral.
Integrate and evaluate using the matching variable and bounds.
pitfalls: Use the factor needed to match du.
Avoid combining x-bounds with a u-integrand.
checks: Differentiate the antiderivative or check the transformed endpoints.

title: Integration by parts
pattern: ∫ u dv = uv−∫ v du.
applies: u and v are differentiable with integrable terms on the interval.
steps: Choose u whose derivative simplifies the expression and dv you can integrate.
Compute du and v.
Apply the formula and simplify the remaining integral.
pitfalls: The remaining integral is subtracted.
For definite integrals, evaluate the uv boundary term at both endpoints.
checks: Differentiate the result and simplify back to the integrand.

example.problem: Find ∫ x ln x dx for x>0.

title: Improper integral by a limit
pattern: Replace every infinite or singular endpoint with a limit of proper integrals.
applies: The integrand is integrable on compact subintervals away from its singularities.
steps: Split the integral at any interior singularity.
Evaluate each proper integral with a variable bound.
Take limits separately and add only when all required integrals converge.
pitfalls: Cancellation across a singularity can give a principal value even when the improper integral diverges.
checks: Check each one-sided limit for a finite value.

title: Power series radius and endpoints
aliases: ratio test for a power series
pattern: Find |x−c|<R first, then test x=c−R and x=c+R separately.
applies: The series is a power series about a fixed center c.
steps: Use the ratio or root test to locate the open convergence interval.
Substitute each finite endpoint into the original series.
State the radius and include only convergent endpoints.
pitfalls: A ratio-test limit of one is inconclusive.
The two endpoints can have different behavior.
checks: Identify the endpoint series explicitly.

example.problem: Find the convergence interval of Σ from n=1 to ∞ of (x−2)^n/(n·3^n).

title: Taylor polynomial at a point
pattern: P_n(x)=Σ from k=0 to n of f^(k)(a)(x−a)^k/k!.
applies: The derivatives through order n exist at the expansion point. An error bound needs additional hypotheses.
steps: Compute f and its derivatives at a.
Divide the kth derivative by k! and use the centered power (x−a)^k.
Sum through the requested degree.
pitfalls: A Taylor polynomial gives a local approximation. Exact equality needs a justified remainder or convergence argument.
checks: The polynomial and function should agree in value and requested derivatives at a.

example.problem: Find the degree-2 Taylor polynomial for √(3+x) at x=1.

title: Gradient and tangent plane to a graph
pattern: z=f(a,b)+f_x(a,b)(x−a)+f_y(a,b)(y−b).
applies: f is differentiable at (a,b). Continuous first partials nearby are a sufficient condition.
steps: Find the point height f(a,b).
Compute and evaluate both first partial derivatives.
Use the height and slopes in the tangent-plane equation.
pitfalls: Evaluate the slopes at the given point.
Hold the other variable fixed when taking each partial.
checks: Substitute x=a and y=b and recover the point height.

example.problem: Find the tangent plane to z=x²y+3y above (2,−1).

title: Lagrange multipliers
pattern: At a regular constrained extremum, ∇f=λ∇g together with g=c.
applies: f and g are differentiable and ∇g is nonzero at the candidate point.
steps: Write the objective and equality constraint.
Solve the gradient equations with the constraint.
Evaluate f at candidates and separately check any singular or boundary cases.
pitfalls: A multiplier solution is a candidate. Existence of global extrema needs justification.
checks: Verify the constraint and compare objective values.

example.problem: Find the extrema of 3x+4y subject to x²+y²=9.

title: Double integration in polar coordinates
pattern: Use x=r cos θ, y=r sin θ and dA=r dr dθ.
applies: The region has a polar description that covers it once except on sets of area zero.
steps: Translate the region into radial and angular bounds.
Rewrite the integrand and include the Jacobian factor r.
Integrate over the transformed region.
pitfalls: The area factor r is required even for a radial integrand.
Check for overlapping angular coverage.
checks: Integrating 1 over the region should give its known area when available.

title: Green’s theorem for circulation
pattern: For positive orientation, ∮(P dx+Q dy)=∬(Q_x−P_y)dA.
applies: The boundary is piecewise smooth and positively oriented. P and Q have continuous first partials on a neighborhood of the region.
steps: Identify the region and verify orientation.
Compute Q_x−P_y.
Integrate that scalar over the region.
pitfalls: Clockwise traversal reverses the sign.
For holes, orient each inner boundary clockwise under the positive-orientation convention.
checks: Check the derivative order and signs before integrating.

title: Separation of variables
pattern: For y′=g(x)h(y), integrate dy/h(y)=g(x)dx where h(y)≠0.
applies: The right-hand side factors into a function of x and a function of y.
Work on an interval where the rearrangement is defined.
steps: Record equilibrium solutions from h(y)=0 before dividing.
Integrate both sides and use the initial condition to find the constant.
Choose the branch and solution interval containing the initial point.
pitfalls: Division by h(y) can omit equilibria.
An algebraic expression can have singularities that restrict its solution interval.
checks: Differentiate the resulting solution and substitute the initial value.

example.problem: Solve y′=2xy² with y(0)=1/3 and find its maximal interval.

title: Integrating factor for a first-order linear ODE
pattern: For y′+p(t)y=q(t), use μ(t)=exp(∫p(t)dt) so (μy)′=μq.
applies: p and q are continuous on the chosen interval after putting the coefficient of y′ equal to one.
steps: Write the equation in standard form and compute μ.
Multiply through by μ and recognize the derivative of μy.
Integrate, divide by μ, and apply any initial condition.
pitfalls: Normalize the leading coefficient before finding p.
Keep the integration constant when solving for y.
checks: Verify the original equation and initial condition directly.

title: Autonomous phase line and stability
pattern: For y′=f(y), equilibria satisfy f(y)=0. The sign of f sets the direction between equilibria.
applies: The autonomous scalar equation has unique local solutions near the equilibria being classified, for example when f is locally Lipschitz.
steps: Find the equilibrium values.
Test the sign of f in each interval they define.
Classify attraction and repulsion from the neighboring arrows.
pitfalls: A zero value of f′ at an equilibrium needs sign analysis.
Attraction from one side only is distinct from two-sided asymptotic stability.
checks: Check that the sign on each side points toward a claimed asymptotically stable equilibrium.

example.answer: y=0 is unstable. y=3 is asymptotically stable.

title: Constant-coefficient homogeneous ODE
pattern: For ay″+by′+cy=0, solve ar²+br+c=0.
applies: The coefficients are constant and a≠0.
steps: Find the characteristic roots and their multiplicities.
Use e^(rt) for a simple real root, e^(rt) and te^(rt) for a repeated real root, or the real sine/cosine pair for conjugate roots.
Use the two initial conditions to determine constants if given.
pitfalls: A repeated root requires a second independent solution.
For complex roots, include the exponential from the real part.
checks: Differentiate and verify both the ODE and the initial data.

example.problem: Solve y″−4y′+4y=0 with y(0)=2 and y′(0)=1.

title: Undetermined coefficients with resonance
pattern: Use y=y_h+y_p. Multiply the standard particular trial by t^s when its characteristic root has multiplicity s.
applies: The ODE is linear with constant coefficients, and the forcing is a finite combination of polynomial, exponential, sine and cosine products.
steps: Solve the homogeneous characteristic equation.
Choose a trial matching the forcing family and adjust for overlap with the homogeneous solution.
Substitute the trial and equate coefficients.
pitfalls: A sine or cosine trial usually needs both phases.
Resonant trials require the power of t given by the root multiplicity.
checks: Apply the differential operator to the particular solution and recover the forcing.

example.problem: Find the general solution of y″+y=2 cos t.
example.answer: y(t)=C₁ cos t+C₂ sin t+t sin t.

title: Laplace transform with a delayed forcing
pattern: L{u(t−a)f(t−a)}=e^(−as)F(s), for a≥0.
applies: The initial value problem starts at t=0 and the transformed functions are piecewise continuous and of exponential order.
steps: Transform the equation using the initial values in each derivative term.
Solve algebraically for Y(s) and factor out any e^(−as) delay.
Invert the undelayed transform and shift its time argument.
pitfalls: The shift applies to the entire time-domain function inside the step.
A factor e^(−as) represents a time delay.
checks: Check the initial value and each interval on either side of the switch.

title: Exact first-order differential equation
pattern: If M_y=N_x on a suitable region, seek F with F_x=M and F_y=N. Solutions lie on F=C.
applies: M and N have continuous first partials on a simply connected open region where the equation is exact.
For a local solution y(x), the implicit equation can be solved near the initial point when F_y≠0.
steps: Check M_y=N_x.
Integrate M with respect to x and include an unknown function of y.
Match F_y to N and use the initial value to fix C.
pitfalls: The integration function can depend on y.
Select the implicit branch passing through the initial point.
checks: Differentiate the potential to recover both coefficients.

example.answer: x²y+3x+2y²=2, on the branch with y(0)=1.

title: Eigenmodes for a constant linear system
pattern: For x′=Ax and a real eigenbasis, x(t)=Σ c_i e^(λ_i t)v_i.
applies: A is constant and has a full real eigenbasis. Other cases use generalized or complex modes.
steps: Compute eigenvalues and a full eigenbasis.
Expand the initial vector in that basis.
Multiply each initial component by its exponential time factor.
pitfalls: Use the eigenvalue corresponding to each eigenvector.
A defective matrix needs additional generalized modes.
checks: At t=0 the modes should sum to the initial vector, and each mode must satisfy x′=Ax.

title: Gaussian elimination for a linear system
pattern: Reduce the augmented matrix [A | b] using elementary row operations.
applies: The equations are linear in the unknowns.
steps: Write one row per equation with a consistent variable order.
Use swaps, nonzero rescaling and row addition to create pivots.
Read the solution, identifying free variables or any contradiction row.
pitfalls: Apply each row operation to the right-hand side as well.
A row of zero coefficients with nonzero right-hand side signals inconsistency.
checks: Substitute any proposed solution into all original equations.

title: Basis from pivot columns
pattern: Pivot column indices in RREF select basis columns from the original matrix.
applies: The vectors are columns of a matrix over the same field.
steps: Place the given vectors as columns of A.
Row-reduce A and record its pivot column indices.
Take the corresponding columns from A as a basis.
pitfalls: The reduced columns generally span a different subspace.
A dependent vector can be omitted even if it is nonzero.
checks: Express omitted vectors as combinations of the selected vectors when practical.

example.problem: Find a basis for the span of (1,0,1), (0,2,1), and (1,4,3).

title: Null space and rank-nullity
pattern: Solve Ax=0. For n columns, rank(A)+dim ker(A)=n.
applies: The system is homogeneous and the number of columns gives the domain dimension.
steps: Row-reduce A.
Write pivot variables in terms of the free variables.
Set each free variable to one in turn with the others zero to obtain basis vectors.
pitfalls: The number of free variables is based on columns rather than rows.
Parameter vectors must satisfy the original homogeneous system.
checks: Verify Av=0 for every basis vector and check the rank-nullity count.

title: Determinant by row operations
pattern: For triangular U, det(U) is the product of its diagonal entries.
applies: A is square and each row operation’s determinant factor can be tracked.
steps: Use row addition and swaps to make A triangular.
Track the determinant multiplier for each swap or rescaling.
Use the triangular determinant and undo the tracked factors.
pitfalls: A row addition leaves the determinant unchanged.
A determinant of zero means the square matrix is singular.
checks: Check the sign against a cofactor expansion or the recorded swap parity.

title: Diagonalization with eigenvectors
pattern: A=PDP^−1 when P has a full set of independent eigenvector columns.
applies: A is square and has a full eigenbasis over the field in use.
steps: Find the eigenvalues from det(A−λI)=0.
Find a basis for each eigenspace.
Place independent eigenvectors in P and their corresponding eigenvalues in D.
pitfalls: Repeated eigenvalues can have too few independent eigenvectors.
Match each eigenvalue to its eigenvector’s column position.
checks: Verify AP=PD and that P is invertible.

title: Gram–Schmidt orthonormalization
pattern: Subtract previous orthogonal projections from each vector, then normalize the residual.
applies: The starting vectors are independent in an inner-product space.
steps: Normalize the first vector.
For each later vector, subtract its projection onto every previous orthonormal vector.
Normalize the remaining vector.
pitfalls: Project onto the orthogonalized vectors, using their correct norm.
A zero residual signals dependence.
checks: Verify pairwise inner products are zero and each output norm is one.

example.problem: Apply Gram–Schmidt to (1,1,0) and (1,0,1), in that order.

title: Orthogonal projection onto a subspace
pattern: For orthogonal basis vectors u_i, proj_W b=Σ ((b·u_i)/(u_i·u_i))u_i.
applies: The basis is orthogonal and its vectors are nonzero.
steps: Compute the coefficient of b along each basis vector.
Add the resulting components.
Form the residual b−proj_W b.
pitfalls: For a non-orthogonal basis, orthonormalize or solve the normal equations first.
The denominator is the squared norm for an orthogonal basis.
checks: Check that the residual is orthogonal to each basis vector.

example.problem: Project b=(3,1,−2) onto the span of (1,1,0) and (0,0,2).

title: Least squares and normal equations
pattern: A least-squares solution satisfies AᵀA x=Aᵀb. QR also gives a solution and avoids forming AᵀA.
applies: The goal is to minimize the Euclidean residual norm. Full column rank gives a unique minimizer.
steps: Build the design matrix A and data vector b.
Solve with QR or solve the normal equations for a small exact problem.
Interpret the coefficients and evaluate the residual.
pitfalls: Include a column of ones for a fitted intercept.
Use QR or SVD for ill-conditioned problems.
checks: Check Aᵀ(b−Ax)=0.

example.problem: Fit y=a+bt by least squares to (0,1), (1,2), and (2,2).

title: Symmetric matrices and positive definiteness
pattern: For real symmetric A, A=QΛQᵀ. The form xᵀAx is positive definite exactly when all eigenvalues are positive.
applies: A is real and symmetric. For a quadratic form, use its symmetric coefficient matrix.
steps: Find the eigenvalues and their signs.
Use an orthonormal eigenbasis when a diagonal form is requested.
Classify the form from the eigenvalue signs.
pitfalls: A zero eigenvalue prevents strict positive definiteness.
Mixed signs give an indefinite form.
checks: Check the eigenvalues using the trace and determinant when helpful.

title: Singular values and singular vectors
pattern: The nonnegative singular values are the square roots of eigenvalues of AᵀA.
applies: A is real and may be rectangular. Use orthonormal eigenvectors of the symmetric matrix AᵀA.
steps: Diagonalize AᵀA and order eigenvalues from largest to smallest.
Set σ_i=√λ_i and let v_i be the corresponding right singular vector.
For σ_i>0, compute u_i=Av_i/σ_i. Complete orthonormal bases if a full SVD is needed.
pitfalls: Use square roots of AᵀA eigenvalues.
A zero singular value needs a separate orthonormal completion.
checks: Verify Av_i=σ_i u_i for every positive singular value.

example.problem: Find the positive singular values and corresponding right singular vectors of [[3,0],[0,0],[0,4]].
example.answer: σ=4 with v=(0,1), and σ=3 with v=(1,0).

title: Coordinates in a chosen basis
pattern: If B=[b₁ … b_n], then v=B[v]_B, so solve Bc=v.
applies: The ordered columns form a basis of the space containing v.
steps: Write the basis vectors as columns in the specified order.
Solve the linear system for the coefficient vector.
Read the coefficients in the same basis order.
pitfalls: Reversing a basis order changes the coordinate tuple.
For standard coordinates from basis coordinates, multiply by B.
checks: Rebuild the original vector as the stated linear combination.

example.problem: Find the coordinates of (5,3) in the ordered basis ((2,1),(1,1)).
